lettered

LET-erd -- from letter (Latin littera, 'letter of the alphabet') plus the suffix -ed ('having, marked by'). · adjective

What It Means

Lettered is having a good education; literate and well-read.

In a village where few people could read at all, the lettered blacksmith was often asked to read letters aloud for his neighbors.

Example

At the veterans' reunion, the quietly lettered mechanic surprised everyone by reciting an entire Robert Frost poem from memory during the toast.

His deep reading and general education -- not his trade -- are what make him lettered.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

learned: Learned means having deep knowledge gained through serious study in some field — law, medicine, history. Lettered is broader and softer: well educated and widely read in general. A learned judge has mastered a discipline; a lettered one has simply read widely and well.

cultivated: Cultivated means refined by education and exposure — polished taste, manners, and conversation. Lettered points specifically at books: schooling and wide reading. A cultivated host may know wine, music, and how to charm a room without being especially lettered.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

ignorant: lacking knowledge or learning

unschooled: lacking formal education or training

Where it sits · how deeply read the person is

literate → lettered → scholarly

literate vs. lettered: Literate is weaker than lettered: a first-grader who can read simple picture books is literate, but a lettered person has gone much further, into a deep education built on wide reading.

scholarly vs. lettered: Scholarly goes further than lettered: a lettered person has read widely and well for its own sake, while a scholarly one pushes into formal, systematic study, mastering the sources and methods of a single field.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — letter: a written character of the alphabet (Latin (littera))

Put it together: Lettered simply means marked by letters -- by education and reading -- built from the everyday word letter plus the suffix -ed, meaning 'having' or 'marked by.'

Use the root in a new word: literacy: The new mayor made adult literacy the centerpiece of her first year in office.

Word Choice

Lettered has an old-fashioned, slightly formal ring to it -- it's most often used to describe someone's overall education and reading, especially in contrast to people around them who had little schooling.
